llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses the problem of adaptive conformal inference, particularly when the data exchangeability assumption is violated, which is common in real-world scenarios. Existing approaches based on online gradient descent (OGD) are often sensitive to learning rate selection. The main contribution is a novel approach for adaptive conformal inference that leverages parameter-free online convex optimization techniques. The proposed method is proven to control long-term miscoverage frequency at a nominal level and demonstrates convincing empirical performance without the need for cumbersome parameter tuning.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology frames adaptive conformal inference as an online quantile estimation problem, specifically learning the (1-α)-quantile of nonconformity scores using pinball loss optimization. Unlike prior methods that rely on online (sub)gradient descent, this work adopts parameter-free online convex optimization techniques based on coin betting. Two specific betting strategies are utilized: the Krichevsky-Trofimov (KT) estimator (Algorithm 1) and the Online Newton Step (ONS) method (Algorithm 2). The core idea involves managing a gambler's wealth based on bets determined by the negation of the subgradients of the pinball loss. The method guarantees sub-linear regret bounds and, under the assumption of bounded nonconformity scores, a long-term coverage guarantee.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The target coverage level was consistently set at 90% (α = 0.1) across all experiments. The proposed betting-based conformal predictors (KT, ONS) were compared against Online Gradient Descent (OGD) and Scale-Free OGD (SF-OGD) with various learning rates. For stock price forecasting, Prophet's native uncertainty quantification tool was also used as a baseline. Experiments were conducted on: 1) a simulated changepoint setting using a linear model with changing coefficients, 2) the Electricity Demand Data (New South Wales) using an AR(3) model for one-step and multi-step (H=5) forecasting, and 3) Stock Prices Data for five major stocks (Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Walmart) over a five-year period, utilizing a Prophet model in log-space for multi-horizon (H=5) forecasting. Performance metrics included global and localized empirical coverage, average and localized prediction set width, and local deviation of interval width.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: A primary limitation is that while the method guarantees correct coverage rate in the limit, it may exhibit slightly lower coverage than the nominal level in finite-sample regimes, although this difference is often small in practice. Another crucial assumption for the theoretical long-term coverage guarantee (Theorem 2.1) is that the nonconformity scores must be bounded; if this assumption is violated, the miscoverage rate can be one. However, the method itself does not require explicit knowledge of this bound. The paper also highlights that existing OGD-based methods suffer from sensitivity to learning rate choices and can yield overly conservative or optimistic prediction sets over time if not tuned properly.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: 1. Fast TTA still depends on norm layers; but modern backbones also contain attention, MLP and convolution blocks whose internal statistics drift. 2. A single hand-crafted state vector (µ,σ, entropy) may not suffice to detect non-covariate shifts such as class prior or semantic drift. 3. Even with FM, per-channel γ,β updates scale linearly with #channels, reducing the speed/energy gain on very wide models (ViT-B/16 has 768-D tokens, Swin-L >1 k). 4. Current energy proxy is heuristic and not tied to hardware-level power counters, giving weak guarantees. 5. No formal guarantee against error amplification; fall-back heuristics may still fail under abrupt or adversarial shifts.
Methods: We propose LANCE (Low-rAnk, Norm- and Component-agnostic Energy-aware adaptation), an extension of FAST-LANA that addresses the above.
A. Universal Adaptive Factors
   • Replace per-channel γ,β with low-rank, token-wise modulators WpWrᵀ (rank r≪C) injected after ANY linear sub-layer (Conv, MatMul, FFN) as y=x+WpWrᵀx.  r=4 keeps <0.5 % extra FLOPs.
   • A single hyper-RNN h_φ outputs ∆Wp,∆Wr given layer summaries.
B. Rich Shift Sensing
   • For every layer we collect a 8-D summary s_t=[µ,σ,Skew,Kurtosis,Entropy,MaxProb,∆losŝ,‖∆θ‖].  ∆losŝ is a one-step look-ahead loss predicted by a tiny zero-cost head trained off-line.
C. Energy-constrained Meta-learning
   • Meta-objective J = CE + λ_E Ê + λ_S ‖∆θ‖² where Ê is estimated Joules via a calibrated regression on NVIDIA power logs; calibration done once per device type (Jetson, RTX).
   • Optimise φ,W* with constrained RL (Lagrangian PPO) to satisfy Ê≤Eₘₐₓ while minimising CE.
D. Drift-safe Controller
   • Maintain an Unscented-Kalman filter on the hidden state of h_φ; if the innovation >δ we revert to last safe parameters and enlarge process noise → faster re-stabilisation.
E. Dataset-free Meta-training
   • Synthetic streams built online using styleGAN-based texture remix + frequency-domain weather engine; no pre-saved corruption lists.
F. Optional Federated Refinement
   • Edge devices periodically send 16-byte sketches (ema of s_t) to update φ without raw data.
All components run in PyTorch and TorchScript for edge deployment.
Experimental Setup: Backbones: ResNet-50-BN, ConvNeXt-T (GN), ViT-B/16 (LN), Swin-T.
Tasks: Image classification on ImageNet-C/R/A, VisDA-C; semantic segmentation on Cityscapes → ACDC-Snow (to test non-covariate, winter shift).
Protocols: Realistic TTA (r∈{50,200} img/s) + new Harsh-Jump (abrupt snow→fog→night every 2 k frames).
Metrics: Top-1, mIoU (seg), Throughput, Energy/img, CO2-eq (via codecarbon), Drift-Δ, Recovery-time after jump.
Devices: Jetson Xavier NX (10 W), RTX-A4000 laptop (mobile).
Experimental Code: class LowRankMod(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, rank=4):
        super().__init__(); self.P=nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(dim,rank)); self.R=nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(rank,dim))
    def forward(self,x,delta):
        P=self.P+delta[:,:self.P.numel()].view_as(self.P)
        R=self.R+delta[:,self.P.numel():].view_as(self.R)
        return x + (x @ R.t()) @ P.t()

class HyperRNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,state_dim, out_dim):
        super().__init__(); self.rnn=nn.GRU(state_dim,32,1); self.fc=nn.Linear(32,out_dim)
        self.h=None
    def forward(self,s): y,self.h=self.rnn(s.unsqueeze(0),self.h); return self.fc(y.squeeze(0))

# device-calibrated energy proxy
class EnergyMeter:
    def __init__(self,device):
        coeff=torch.load(f"calib_{device}.pt")  # linear reg coefficients
        self.a,self.b=coeff
    def __call__(self,flops,mem): return self.a*flops + self.b*mem

Expected Result: • ≤0.7 % drop vs 5-step Tent on all shifts; >3 % gain over FAST-LANA on sudden jumps.
• 7× speed-up and 65 % energy saving vs 5-step Tent; 15 % extra saving over FAST-LANA due to low-rank factors.
• First fast TTA to keep ViT-B within 9 W average on Xavier; meets 10 W power envelope.
• After a synthetic snow→night jump, accuracy recovers within 150 images (vs 600 for FAST-LANA, >2000 for Tent).
• Federated refinement improves average OOD accuracy by +0.6 % after 3 edge rounds, with <5 kB uplink.
Expected Conclusion: LANCE demonstrates that low-rank, component-agnostic modulators controlled by an energy-aware hyper-RNN enable reliable, green and drift-safe test-time adaptation on modern architectures—even under abrupt non-covariate shocks—without any backward pass. It extends the TTA toolbox beyond norm layers, integrates formal energy constraints, and shows how federated sketches can continually refine adaptation without sharing data, pushing TTA towards scalable, privacy-respectful deployment on heterogeneous edge hardware.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
EXP-1  Unified Accuracy / Speed / Energy Benchmark
Goal: Show that LANCE simultaneously (a) matches or exceeds state-of-the-art OOD accuracy, (b) reaches real-time throughput and (c) respects a strict energy budget on a single NVIDIA A100.

Protocol
1. Backbones: ResNet-50-BN, ConvNeXt-T (GN), ViT-B/16 (LN), Swin-T.
2. Test streams (≈100 k frames each, shuffled once):  • ImageNet-C (15 severities)  • ImageNet-R  • VisDA-C  • Cityscapes → ACDC-Snow.
3. Streaming rate: 50 img/s and 200 img/s (simulate edge batch sizes 1 and 4).
4. Methods:   a) LANCE   b) FAST-LANA   c) Tent-5-step   d) Source-only.
5. Instrumentation:  • NVML power logger (1 kHz)  • CodeCarbon for CO₂-eq  • PyTorch profiler for FLOPs.
6. Measured metrics:  Top-1 / mIoU, images · s⁻¹, mean Joules · img⁻¹, peak power, CO₂-eq, memory.

Expected Outcome
• LANCE ≤0.7 % behind Tent-5-step in accuracy, +3 % over FAST-LANA on all streams.
• 7× faster and 65 % lower energy/img than Tent; 15 % energy saving over FAST-LANA through low-rank factors.
• Keeps ViT-B/16 under 150 W (A100 low-power mode) while Tent exceeds 300 W.
Demonstrates that the proposed universal low-rank modulators and energy-aware hyper-RNN yield state-of-the-art accuracy without sacrificing real-time constraints or power efficiency.

-------------------------------------------------------------
EXP-2  Component Ablation & Scaling Analysis
Goal: Quantify the individual contribution of each LANCE component and verify sub-linear parameter/compute scaling on very wide models.

Protocol
1. Backbone family sweep: ViT-S (384D tokens) → ViT-L (1024D) and Swin-L (1 k+ channels).
2. LANCE variants:
   A) full model (baseline)
   B) no energy constraint (λ_E=0)
   C) replace low-rank WₚWᵣᵀ with per-channel γ,β
   D) remove UKF drift controller
   E) static (non-recurrent) hyper-net.
3. Dataset: ImageNet-C @ severity 3 streamed 30 k frames.
4. Record: accuracy, adaptation FLOPs, extra parameters, energy/img, recovery time after a synthetic snow→night jump.

Expected Outcome
• Low-rank factors divide adaptation FLOPs and parameters by >20× on ViT-L while preserving accuracy (drop <0.4 %).
• Energy-constrained objective cuts power by ≈12 % at <0.2 % accuracy loss; omitting it violates 200 W cap.
• UKF controller halves post-jump recovery time (150→310 images).
• Replacing the hyper-RNN by a static mapper costs ≈1.3 % accuracy.
Shows that every listed innovation is necessary; especially, universality & low-rankness solve Problem 1 & 3, and the energy term solves Problem 4.

-------------------------------------------------------------
EXP-3  Robustness Stress-Test: Harsh-Jump & Adversarial Drift
Goal: Validate formal drift-safety (Problem 5) under worst-case shifts.

Protocol
1. Continuous 40 k-frame stream, distribution order: clean → fog → PGD-ε4 adversarial → snow → night; shift every 2 k frames.
2. Methods: LANCE vs FAST-LANA vs Tent (single-step for speed) vs BN-adapt.
3. Inject white-box PGD attacks crafted against the current adapted model (3 steps, ε=4/255) during the adversarial segment.
4. Log per-frame Top-1, innovation magnitude, rollback events, and cumulative error.

Expected Outcome
• LANCE triggers ≤3 rollbacks, never exceeds 15 consecutive frames with Top-1<20 %, and fully recovers within 150 frames after each shift.
• FAST-LANA requires >600 frames, Tent fails (diverges) under PGD.
• Innovation statistics correlate (ρ>0.8) with accuracy drop, validating the UKF safety filter.
Demonstrates formal drift-safe behaviour and protection against error amplification even under adversarial, non-covariate shocks.

-------------------------------------------------------------
Combined, these three experiments illustrate LANCE’s effectiveness from complementary angles: (1) practical performance & efficiency, (2) internal design justification and scaling, and (3) robustness & safety under extreme distribution dynamics.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
====================================================
GLOBAL SETTINGS (apply to all three experiments)
----------------------------------------------------
Hardware & Software
• Node : 1 × NVIDIA A100-80 GB, AMD EPYC 7763, 2 TB RAM.  
• Framework : PyTorch 2.1 + TorchVision 0.17, CUDA 12.2, cudnn 8.9, NCCL 2.18.  
• Mixed-precision : bfloat16 autocast; gradient-scaled to keep UKF matrices in FP32.  
• Determinism : torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic=True; seeds {13, 37, 97}.  
• Logging : MLflow + Weights & Biases, NVML (1 kHz) + CodeCarbon 2.3.2, PyTorch profiler.  
• FLOP counter : fvcore’s FlopCountAnalysis patched for ViT/Swin.

Source-Training Checkpoints (common)
• ResNet-50-BN                 : ImageNet-1 k pre-trained (torchvision).  
• ConvNeXt-T (GN)              : ConvNeXt-T @ 224 px (facebookresearch).  
• ViT-B/16, ViT-S/16, ViT-L/16 : timm pre-trained weights.  
• Swin-T / Swin-L              : timm pre-trained weights.  
• Segmentation heads           : DeepLab-v3+ with the same encoder, trained on Cityscapes train (fine) for 80 k it., poly LR schedule.

General Pre-processing
CLS (ImageNet/VisDA-C/R):
1. Resize shortest side→256; center-crop 224; for ViT 224×224 patchify.
2. ToTensor → Normalise with ImageNet mean/std.
SEG (Cityscapes/ACDC):
1. Resize to 1024×2048; random horizontal flip (training only); normalise per-channel mean/std from Cityscapes train.

Data Splits (for evaluation only)
• ImageNet-val (50 k) → OOD corruptions form the test streams (no labels used during adaptation).  
• VisDA-C validation split (all 55 k images).  
• Cityscapes val (500), ACDC-Snow test (4 k). Labels kept for post-stream evaluation only.

Metric Conventions
Primary   : Top-1 accuracy (classification), mIoU (segmentation).  
Secondary : AUROC (OOD vs ID), Energy/img (J), Images/s, Peak-Power (W), CO₂-eq (g), ECE (expected calib. error).
Selection : Report mean ± std over 3 seeds; main tables use last-checkpoint (online TTA), appendix gives best-val (retrospective) for transparency.
Early stop : N/A (streaming TTA never sees labels).

Hyper-parameter Grid (for sensitivity analysis, §5 in each exp.)
• Rank r ∈ {2,4,8}.  
• λ_E ∈ {0,0.5,1,2}.  
• UKF innovation threshold δ ∈ {1,2,3} σ above running mean.  
• RNN hidden size ∈ {16,32,64}.  
Grid executed on a 2-hour slice of ImageNet-C (severity 3); best λ_E,r,δ used in main runs.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
EXP-1  Unified Accuracy / Speed / Energy Benchmark
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Goal  : joint evaluation of accuracy, throughput, energy under realistic streaming.

1. Backbones & Variants (4 encoders × 4 methods)
   a. LANCE (ours)
   b. FAST-LANA (Hu et al. 2023) – reproduced with authors’ config†
   c. Tent-5-step (Wang et al. 2021)
   d. Source-only (frozen)
   († we disable CUDA graph due to A100 kernel launch limits, +5 ms/iter, noted in appendix.)

2. Datasets / Streams (≈100 k frames each)
   • ImageNet-C (15 types × 5 severity, looped)            – cls
   • ImageNet-R                                           – cls
   • VisDA-C (validation)                                 – cls
   • Cityscapes → ACDC-Snow (concatenated)                – seg
Streaming order is randomly shuffled once, fixed across seeds. Two replay speeds: 50 fps (batch=1) & 200 fps (batch=4, gradient-acc. off).

3. Evaluation Protocol
   • Run each (backbone,method,speed) tuple for the full 100 k-frame stream.
   • Record on-line per-frame metrics; summarise by the mean of final 20 % of frames (steady state).
   • Energy/img = ∑Joules / #frames, measured by NVML average of 10 ms windows.
   • ECE: 15-bin adaptive hist., computed offline per 10 k-frame chunk.
   • Throughput measured by avg wall-clock excluding initial model load.

4. Robustness & Noise
   • Add Gaussian sensor noise N(0,0.03) to 10 % of frames to test resilience; report accuracy drop.

5. Hyper-parameter Analysis
   • During a dedicated pilot run (ImageNet-C @ severity3, 5 k frames) sweep λ_E & r. Acc/Energy Pareto curve plotted.

6. Compute & Cost Reporting
   • PyTorch profiler with schedule (wait 500, warm up 500, active 1 k iter) gives FLOPs and CPU time.
   • Memory peak via torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated().
   • Cost: AWS p4d.24xlarge pricing (≈ $32/h) * runtime.

7. Example Code Snippet (adaptation loop)
```python
meter = EnergyMeter('A100')
for i,(imgs,_) in enumerate(stream_loader):
    with torch.autocast('cuda','bfloat16'):
        outs = model(imgs)
        state = collect_state(outs, model)        # µ,σ,… 8-D
        delta  = hyper_rnn(state)
        apply_low_rank(model, delta)              # Wp,Wr update
    flops = profiled_flops(outs)
    energy = meter(flops, imgs.numel()*4)         # bytes→J
    log_metrics(i, outs, energy)
```

Expected Tables (§4.1 of paper)
• Accuracy/mIoU vs Energy/img for each speed.  
• Images/s vs Peak power.  
• CO₂-eq (g) / 1 k images.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
EXP-2  Component Ablation & Scaling Analysis
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Goal  : quantify each module’s benefit and show sub-linear scaling on wide models.

1. Models
   Encoders : ViT-S/16 (384-D), ViT-B/16 (768-D), ViT-L/16 (1024-D), Swin-L (1056-C).  
   LANCE Variants :
   A) full (default)            
   B) λ_E = 0 (no energy constraint)  
   C) per-channel γ,β instead of low-rank  
   D) −UKF (simple running-mean)  
   E) MLP-hyper (no RNN)

2. Dataset & Stream
   • ImageNet-C, severity 3, 30 k frames @ 50 fps.  
   • Inject synthetic snow→night jump at frame 15 k.

3. Measurements
   • Accuracy drop across width.  
   • Additional parameters (adaptation-specific) = |Wp|+|Wr|+|φ| etc.  
   • Adaptation FLOPs per frame.  
   • Joules/img and whether 200 W cap violated.  
   • Recovery time (#frames until accuracy within 90 % of pre-jump level).

4. Hyper-parameter Sensitivity
   • r={2,4,8} for ViT-L; plot FLOPs vs Top-1.  
   • Hidden-size={16,32,64}.

5. Robustness Check
   • Repeat snow→night jump with an extra additive brightness drift (+30 %) to evaluate controller robustness.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
EXP-3  Robustness Stress-Test: Harsh-Jump & Adversarial Drift
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Goal  : verify drift-safe controller under worst-case distribution shifts.

1. Stream (40 k frames, 50 fps)
   Segment-length 2 k frames, order: clean → fog (C-fog-3) → PGD (ε=4/255, 3-steps, ℓ∞) → snow (C-snow-4) → night (geometric darkening). Attacks crafted online on the current adapted model.

2. Methods Compared
   • LANCE (ours)  
   • FAST-LANA  
   • Tent-1-step (to meet speed)  
   • BN-adapt (BatchNorm stats replacement)

3. Metrics
   • Per-frame Top-1.  
   • Innovation magnitude (UKF).  
   • #Rollback events + frames lost.  
   • Cumulative error AUC (∫𝟙[pred≠y] over time).  
   • Attack success rate.  
   • ECE drift.

4. Robustness Analyses
   a. Noise Injection : randomly add speckle noise every 100 th frame.  
   b. Distribution Shift : swap segment order in a second run; measure whether UKF false-positives rise.  
   c. Adversarial Strength Sweep : ε∈{2/255,4/255,8/255}.

5. Safety Threshold Study
   • δ∈{1,2,3}σ; plot false-rollback vs missed-drift trade-off.

6. Compute Overhead
   • Measure extra µs for UKF + predict-loss head per frame (<0.08 ms expected).

----------------------------------------------------------------------
COMMON ROBUSTNESS & STATISTICAL PRACTICES
----------------------------------------------------------------------
• All numeric claims accompanied by 95 % CIs (t-distribution over 3 seeds).  
• We test homoscedasticity (Levene) before t-tests when comparing LANCE vs FAST-LANA.  
• Significance threshold α=0.05, Holm-Bonferroni over metrics.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
FAIL-FAST POLICY (NO-FALLBACK)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
If any dataset cannot be downloaded (e.g., ImageNet license lost), the script terminates with:
```bash
raise RuntimeError('Dataset unavailable – experiment aborted as per NO-FALLBACK constraint.')
```
No synthetic placeholders will be substituted.

# Model card for resnet50.a1_in1k

A ResNet-B image classification model.

This model features:
 * ReLU activations
 * single layer 7x7 convolution with pooling
 * 1x1 convolution shortcut downsample

Trained on ImageNet-1k in `timm` using recipe template described below.

Recipe details:
 * ResNet Strikes Back `A1` recipe
 * LAMB optimizer with BCE loss
 * Cosine LR schedule with warmup


## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 25.6
  - GMACs: 4.1
  - Activations (M): 11.1
  - Image size: train = 224 x 224, test = 288 x 288
- **Papers:**
  - ResNet strikes back: An improved training procedure in timm: https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00476
  - Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385
- **Original:** https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm
import torch

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('resnet50.a1_in1k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Feature Map Extraction
```python

    pretrained=True,
    features_only=True,
)

transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

for o in output:

    #  torch.Size([1, 512, 28, 28])
    #  torch.Size([1, 1024, 14, 14])
    #  torch.Size([1, 2048, 7, 7])

    print(o.shape)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model(
    'resnet50.a1_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor

# or equivalently (without needing to set num_classes=0)

output = model.forward_features(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))
# output is unpooled, a (1, 2048, 7, 7) shaped tensor

output = model.forward_head(output, pre_logits=True)
# output is a (1, num_features) shaped tensor
```

# ResNet-50 v1.5

ResNet model pre-trained on ImageNet-1k at resolution 224x224. It was introduced in the paper [Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) by He et al. 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ResNet did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

ResNet (Residual Network) is a convolutional neural network that democratized the concepts of residual learning and skip connections. This enables to train much deeper models.

This is ResNet v1.5, which differs from the original model: in the bottleneck blocks which require downsampling, v1 has stride = 2 in the first 1x1 convolution, whereas v1.5 has stride = 2 in the 3x3 convolution. This difference makes ResNet50 v1.5 slightly more accurate (\~0.5% top1) than v1, but comes with a small performance drawback (~5% imgs/sec) according to [Nvidia](https://catalog.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/nvidia/resources/resnet_50_v1_5_for_pytorch).

![model image](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/resnet_architecture.png)

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=resnet) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, ResNetForImageClassification
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("huggingface/cats-image")
image = dataset["test"]["image"][0]

processor = AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained("microsoft/resnet-50")
model = ResNetForImageClassification.from_pretrained("microsoft/resnet-50")

inputs = processor(image, return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(**inputs).logits

# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_label = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print(model.config.id2label[predicted_label])
```

For more code examples, we refer to the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/resnet).

```bibtex
}
```

# Model card for resnetv2_50x1_bit.goog_in21k

A ResNet-V2-BiT (Big Transfer w/ pre-activation ResNet) image classification model. Trained on ImageNet-21k by paper authors.

This model uses:
* Group Normalization (GN) in combination with Weight Standardization (WS) instead of Batch Normalization (BN)..


## Model Details
- **Model Type:** Image classification / feature backbone
- **Model Stats:**
  - Params (M): 68.3
  - GMACs: 4.3
  - Activations (M): 11.1
  - Image size: 224 x 224
- **Papers:**
  - Big Transfer (BiT): General Visual Representation Learning: https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.11370
  - Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks: https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05027
- **Dataset:** ImageNet-21k
- **Original:** https://github.com/google-research/big_transfer

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from PIL import Image
import timm

img = Image.open(urlopen(
    'https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/beignets-task-guide.png'
))

model = timm.create_model('resnetv2_50x1_bit.goog_in21k', pretrained=True)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Feature Map Extraction

# ConvNeXt V2 (tiny-sized model) 

ConvNeXt V2 model pretrained using the FCMAE framework and fine-tuned on the ImageNet-22K dataset at resolution 224x224. It was introduced in the paper [ConvNeXt V2: Co-designing and Scaling ConvNets with Masked Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00808) by Woo et al. and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ConvNeXt-V2). 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ConvNeXT V2 did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

ConvNeXt V2 is a pure convolutional model (ConvNet) that introduces a fully convolutional masked autoencoder framework (FCMAE) and a new Global Response Normalization (GRN) layer to ConvNeXt. ConvNeXt V2 significantly improves the performance of pure ConvNets on various recognition benchmarks.

![model image](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/convnextv2_architecture.png)

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=convnextv2) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, ConvNextV2ForImageClassification
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("huggingface/cats-image")
image = dataset["test"]["image"][0]

preprocessor = AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained("facebook/convnextv2-tiny-22k-224")
model = ConvNextV2ForImageClassification.from_pretrained("facebook/convnextv2-tiny-22k-224")

inputs = preprocessor(image, return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(**inputs).logits

# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_label = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print(model.config.id2label[predicted_label]),
```

For more code examples, we refer to the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/master/en/model_doc/convnextv2).

# Vision Transformer (base-sized model) 

Vision Transformer (ViT) model pre-trained on ImageNet-21k (14 million images, 21,843 classes) at resolution 224x224, and fine-tuned on ImageNet 2012 (1 million images, 1,000 classes) at resolution 224x224. It was introduced in the paper [An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) by Dosovitskiy et al. and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/google-research/vision_transformer). However, the weights were converted from the [timm repository](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models) by Ross Wightman, who already converted the weights from JAX to PyTorch. Credits go to him. 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ViT did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

The Vision Transformer (ViT) is a transformer encoder model (BERT-like) pretrained on a large collection of images in a supervised fashion, namely ImageNet-21k, at a resolution of 224x224 pixels. Next, the model was fine-tuned on ImageNet (also referred to as ILSVRC2012), a dataset comprising 1 million images and 1,000 classes, also at resolution 224x224.

Images are presented to the model as a sequence of fixed-size patches (resolution 16x16), which are linearly embedded. One also adds a [CLS] token to the beginning of a sequence to use it for classification tasks. One also adds absolute position embeddings before feeding the sequence to the layers of the Transformer encoder.

By pre-training the model, it learns an inner representation of images that can then be used to extract features useful for downstream tasks: if you have a dataset of labeled images for instance, you can train a standard classifier by placing a linear layer on top of the pre-trained encoder. One typically places a linear layer on top of the [CLS] token, as the last hidden state of this token can be seen as a representation of an entire image.

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=google/vit) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import ViTImageProcessor, ViTForImageClassification
from PIL import Image
import requests

url = 'http://images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000039769.jpg'
image = Image.open(requests.get(url, stream=True).raw)

processor = ViTImageProcessor.from_pretrained('google/vit-base-patch16-224')
model = ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained('google/vit-base-patch16-224')

inputs = processor(images=image, return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model(**inputs)
logits = outputs.logits
# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_class_idx = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print("Predicted class:", model.config.id2label[predicted_class_idx])
```

For more code examples, we refer to the [documentation](https://huggingface.co/transformers/model_doc/vit.html#).

## Training data

## Model Usage
### Image Classification
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen

))

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # unsqueeze single image into batch of 1

top5_probabilities, top5_class_indices = torch.topk(output.softmax(dim=1) * 100, k=5)
```

### Image Embeddings
```python

    'vit_small_patch16_224.augreg_in21k_ft_in1k',
    pretrained=True,
    num_classes=0,  # remove classifier nn.Linear
)
model = model.eval()

# get model specific transforms (normalization, resize)
data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)

output = model(transforms(img).unsqueeze(0))  # output is (batch_size, num_features) shaped tensor
```

# Vision Transformer (large-sized model) 

Vision Transformer (ViT) model pre-trained on ImageNet-21k (14 million images, 21,843 classes) at resolution 224x224, and fine-tuned on ImageNet 2012 (1 million images, 1,000 classes) at resolution 224x224. It was introduced in the paper [An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) by Dosovitskiy et al. and first released in [this repository](https://github.com/google-research/vision_transformer). However, the weights were converted from the [timm repository](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models) by Ross Wightman, who already converted the weights from JAX to PyTorch. Credits go to him. 

Disclaimer: The team releasing ViT did not write a model card for this model so this model card has been written by the Hugging Face team.

## Model description

The Vision Transformer (ViT) is a transformer encoder model (BERT-like) pretrained on a large collection of images in a supervised fashion, namely ImageNet-21k, at a resolution of 224x224 pixels. Next, the model was fine-tuned on ImageNet (also referred to as ILSVRC2012), a dataset comprising 1 million images and 1,000 classes, at the same resolution, 224x224.

Images are presented to the model as a sequence of fixed-size patches (resolution 16x16), which are linearly embedded. One also adds a [CLS] token to the beginning of a sequence to use it for classification tasks. One also adds absolute position embeddings before feeding the sequence to the layers of the Transformer encoder.

By pre-training the model, it learns an inner representation of images that can then be used to extract features useful for downstream tasks: if you have a dataset of labeled images for instance, you can train a standard classifier by placing a linear layer on top of the pre-trained encoder. One typically places a linear layer on top of the [CLS] token, as the last hidden state of this token can be seen as a representation of an entire image.

## Intended uses & limitations

You can use the raw model for image classification. See the [model hub](https://huggingface.co/models?search=google/vit) to look for
fine-tuned versions on a task that interests you.

### How to use

Here is how to use this model to classify an image of the COCO 2017 dataset into one of the 1,000 ImageNet classes:

```python
from transformers import ViTFeatureExtractor, ViTForImageClassification
from PIL import Image
import requests
url = 'http://images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000039769.jpg'
image = Image.open(requests.get(url, stream=True).raw)
feature_extractor = ViTFeatureExtractor.from_pretrained('google/vit-large-patch16-224')
model = ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained('google/vit-large-patch16-224')
inputs = feature_extractor(images=image, return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model(**inputs)
logits = outputs.logits
# model predicts one of the 1000 ImageNet classes
predicted_class_idx = logits.argmax(-1).item()
print("Predicted class:", model.config.id2label[predicted_class_idx])
```

Currently, both the feature extractor and model  support PyTorch. Tensorflow and JAX/FLAX are coming soon, and the API of ViTFeatureExtractor might change.

## Training data

The ViT model was pretrained on [ImageNet-21k](http://www.image-net.org/), a dataset consisting of 14 million images and 21k classes, and fine-tuned on [ImageNet](http://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/2012/), a dataset consisting of 1 million images and 1k classes. 

## Training procedure

### Preprocessing

The exact details of preprocessing of images during training/validation can be found [here](https://github.com/google-research/vision_transformer/blob/master/vit_jax/input_pipeline.py). 

Images are resized/rescaled to the same resolution (224x224) and normalized across the RGB channels with mean (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) and standard deviation (0.5, 0.5, 0.5).

### Pretraining

The model was trained on TPUv3 hardware (8 cores). All model variants are trained with a batch size of 4096 and learning rate warmup of 10k steps. For ImageNet, the authors found it beneficial to additionally apply gradient clipping at global norm 1. Pre-training resolution is 224.

## Evaluation results

For evaluation results on several image classification benchmarks, we refer to tables 2 and 5 of the original paper. Note that for fine-tuning, the best results are obtained with a higher resolution (384x384). Of course, increasing the model size will result in better performance.

# Repack Information

This repository contains a complete repack of [ILSVRC/imagenet-1k](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ILSVRC/imagenet-1k/) in Parquet format with the following data transformations:

1. Images were center-cropped to square to the minimum height/width dimension.
2. Images were then rescaled to 256x256 using Lanczos resampling.

### Dataset Summary

ILSVRC 2012, commonly known as 'ImageNet' is an image dataset organized according to the WordNet hierarchy. Each meaningful concept in WordNet, possibly described by multiple words or word phrases, is called a "synonym set" or "synset". There are more than 100,000 synsets in WordNet, majority of them are nouns (80,000+). ImageNet aims to provide on average 1000 images to illustrate each synset. Images of each concept are quality-controlled and human-annotated.

💡 This dataset provides access to ImageNet (ILSVRC) 2012 which is the most commonly used **subset** of ImageNet. This dataset spans 1000 object classes and contains 1,281,167 training images, 50,000 validation images and 100,000 test images. The version also has the [patch](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16RYnHpVOW0XKCsn3G3S9GTHUyoV2-4WX/view) which fixes some of the corrupted test set images already applied. For full ImageNet dataset presented in [[2]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5206848), please check the download section of the [main website](https://image-net.org/download-images.php).

### Supported Tasks and Leaderboards

- `image-classification`: The goal of this task is to classify a given image into one of 1000 ImageNet classes. The leaderboard is available [here](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/image-classification-on-imagenet?tag_filter=171).

To evaluate the `imagenet-classification` accuracy on the test split, one must first create an account at https://image-net.org. This account must be approved by the site administrator. After the account is created, one can submit the results to the test server at https://image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/eval_server.php The submission consists of several ASCII text files corresponding to multiple tasks. The task of interest is "Classification submission (top-5 cls error)". A sample of an exported text file looks like the following:

```
670 778 794 387 650
217 691 564 909 364
737 369 430 531 124
755 930 755 512 152
```

The export format is described in full in "readme.txt" within the 2013 development kit available here: https://image-net.org/data/ILSVRC/2013/ILSVRC2013_devkit.tgz. Please see the section entitled "3.3 CLS-LOC submission format". Briefly, the format of the text file is 100,000 lines corresponding to each image in the test split. Each line of integers correspond to the rank-ordered, top 5 predictions for each test image. The integers are 1-indexed corresponding to the line number in the corresponding labels file. See `imagenet2012_labels.txt`.

### Languages

The class labels in the dataset are in English.

## Dataset Structure

### Data Instances

An example looks like below: 

```
{
  'image': <PIL.JpegImagePlugin.JpegImageFile image mode=RGB size=384x512 at 0x276021C5EB8>,
  'label': 23
}
```

### Data Fields

The data instances have the following fields:

- `image`: A `PIL.Image.Image` object containing the image. Note that when accessing the image column: `dataset[0]["image"]` the image file is automatically decoded. Decoding of a large number of image files might take a significant amount of time. Thus it is important to first query the sample index before the `"image"` column, *i.e.* `dataset[0]["image"]` should **always** be preferred over `dataset["image"][0]`.
- `label`: an `int` classification label. -1 for `test` set as the labels are missing.

The labels are indexed based on a sorted list of synset ids such as `n07565083` which we automatically map to original class names. The original dataset is divided into folders based on these synset ids. To get a mapping from original synset names, use the file [LOC_synset_mapping.txt](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/imagenet-object-localization-challenge/data?select=LOC_synset_mapping.txt) available on Kaggle challenge page. You can also use `dataset_instance.features["labels"].int2str` function to get the class for a particular label index. Also note that, labels for test set are returned as -1 as they are missing.

## Dataset Creation

### Curation Rationale

The ImageNet project was inspired by two important needs in computer vision research. The first was the need to establish a clear North Star problem in computer vision. While the field enjoyed an abundance of important tasks to work on, from stereo vision to image retrieval, from 3D reconstruction to image segmentation, object categorization was recognized to be one of the most fundamental capabilities of both human and machine vision. Hence there was a growing demand for a high quality object categorization benchmark with clearly established evaluation metrics. Second, there was a critical need for more data to enable more generalizable machine learning methods. Ever since the birth of the digital era and the availability of web-scale data exchanges, researchers in these fields have been working hard to design more and more sophisticated algorithms to index, retrieve, organize and annotate multimedia data. But good research requires good resources. To tackle this problem at scale (think of your growing personal collection of digital images, or videos, or a commercial web search engine’s database), it was critical to provide researchers with a large-scale image database for both training and testing. The convergence of these two intellectual reasons motivated us to build ImageNet.

### Source Data

#### Initial Data Collection and Normalization

Initial data for ImageNet image classification task consists of photographs collected from [Flickr](https://www.flickr.com) and other search engines, manually labeled with the presence of one of 1000 object categories. Constructing ImageNet was an effort to scale up an image classification dataset to cover most nouns in English using tens of millions of manually verified photographs [1](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5206848). The image classification task of ILSVRC came as a direct extension of this effort. A subset of categories and images was chosen and fixed to provide a standardized benchmark while the rest of ImageNet continued to grow.

#### Who are the source language producers?

WordNet synsets further quality controlled by human annotators. The images are from Flickr.

### Annotations

#### Annotation process

The annotation process of collecting ImageNet for image classification task is a three step process.

1. Defining the 1000 object categories for the image classification task. These categories have evolved over the years.
1. Collecting the candidate image for these object categories using a search engine.
1. Quality control on the candidate images by using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) to make sure the image has the synset it was collected for.

See the section 3.1 in [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575) for more details on data collection procedure and [2](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5206848) for general information on ImageNet.

#### Who are the annotators?

Images are automatically fetched from an image search engine based on the synsets and filtered using human annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk. See [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575) for more details.

### Personal and Sensitive Information

The 1,000 categories selected for this subset contain only 3 people categories (scuba diver, bridegroom, and baseball player) while the full ImageNet contains 2,832 people categories under the person subtree (accounting for roughly 8.3% of the total images). This subset does contain the images of people without their consent. Though, the study in [[1]](https://image-net.org/face-obfuscation/) on obfuscating faces of the people in the ImageNet 2012 subset shows that blurring people's faces causes a very minor decrease in accuracy (~0.6%) suggesting that privacy-aware models can be trained on ImageNet. On larger ImageNet, there has been [an attempt](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07726) at filtering and balancing the people subtree in the larger ImageNet.

## Considerations for Using the Data

### Social Impact of Dataset

The ImageNet dataset has been very crucial in advancement of deep learning technology as being the standard benchmark for the computer vision models. The dataset aims to probe models on their understanding of the objects and has become the de-facto dataset for this purpose. ImageNet is still one of the major datasets on which models are evaluated for their generalization in computer vision capabilities as the field moves towards self-supervised algorithms. Please see the future section in [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575) for a discussion on social impact of the dataset.

### Discussion of Biases

1. A [study](https://image-net.org/update-sep-17-2019.php) of the history of the multiple layers (taxonomy, object classes and labeling) of ImageNet and WordNet in 2019 described how bias is deeply embedded in most classification approaches for of all sorts of images.
1. A [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.12231) has also shown that ImageNet trained models are biased towards texture rather than shapes which in contrast with how humans do object classification. Increasing the shape bias improves the accuracy and robustness.
1. Another [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13228) more potential issues and biases with the ImageNet dataset and provides an alternative benchmark for image classification task. The data collected contains humans without their consent.
1. ImageNet data with face obfuscation is also provided at [this link](https://image-net.org/face-obfuscation/)
1. A study on genealogy of ImageNet is can be found at [this link](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20539517211035955) about the "norms, values, and assumptions" in ImageNet.
1. See [this study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07726) on filtering and balancing the distribution of people subtree in the larger complete ImageNet.

### Other Known Limitations

1. Since most of the images were collected from internet, keep in mind that some images in ImageNet might be subject to copyrights. See the following papers for more details: [[1]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.13228) [[2]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0575) [[3]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5206848).

# Imagenet-1K-VL-Enriched

An enriched version of the ImageNet-1K Dataset with image caption, bounding boxes, and label issues!
With this additional information, the ImageNet-1K dataset can be extended to various tasks such as image retrieval or visual question answering.

The label issues helps to curate a cleaner and leaner dataset.

## Description
The dataset consists of 6 columns:

+ `image_id`: The original filename of the image from ImageNet-1K dataset.
+ `image`: Image data in the form of PIL Image.
+ `label`: Label for the image, provided by the authors of the ImageNet-1K dataset.
+ `label_bbox_enriched`: Enriched labels for the image. Consists of bounding box coordinates, confidence scores, and labels for the bounding box generated using object detection models.
+ `caption_enriched`: Enriched captions for the image. Generated by BLIP2 captioning model.
+ `issues`: Quality issues found such as duplicate, mislabeled, dark, blurry, bright, and outlier images.
## Usage
This dataset can be used with the Hugging Face Datasets library.:
```python
import datasets
ds = datasets.load_dataset("visual-layer/imagenet-1k-vl-enriched")
```

More in this [notebook](usage.ipynb).

# Dataset Card for "imagenet_1k_resized_256"

## Dataset summary
The same ImageNet dataset but all the smaller side resized to 256. 
A lot of pretraining workflows contain resizing images to 256 and random cropping to 224x224, this is why 256 is chosen. 
The resized dataset can also be downloaded much faster and consume less space than the original one.
See [here](https://huggingface.co/datasets/imagenet-1k) for detailed readme.

Below is the example of one row of data. Note that the labels in the test split are all -1.

```
  'label': 23
}
```

# ImageNet-R


This repo is made to facilitate the evaluation of various pretraining models. It's constructed from the source file provided by [official implementation](https://github.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r).


## Usage

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset('axiong/imagenet-r')
```


## Dataset Summary


ImageNet-R(endition) contains art, cartoons, deviantart, graffiti, embroidery, graphics, origami, paintings, patterns, plastic objects, plush objects, sculptures, sketches, tattoos, toys, and video game renditions of ImageNet classes.

ImageNet-R has renditions of 200 ImageNet classes resulting in 30,000 images.

[ImageNet-R](https://github.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r) is a dataset proposed on ICCV 2021 by Dan Hendrycks, Steven Basart, Norman Mu, Saurav Kadavath, Frank Wang, Evan Dorundo, Rahul Desai, Tyler Zhu, Samyak Parajuli, Mike Guo, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt and Justin Gilme.
The detailed introduction could be found in their paper 'The Many` Faces of Robustness: A Critical Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Generalization'.

![image/jpg](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hendrycks/imagenet-r/master/yes.jpg)


## Example Data

- `wnid` is the ID from wordnet, used to indicate the class label.
- `class_name` is the the corresponding class name of `wnid`


```json
[
  {
    "image": <PIL Image>,
    "wnid": "n02088094",
    "class_name": "afghan_hound"
  },
  {
    "image": <PIL Image>,
    "wnid": "n07697537",
    "class_name": "hotdog"
  }
]
```

idea.open_problems: Key challenge: Current Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods require several backward passes per batch to converge.  Under realistic, constant-speed data streams this latency means that only a fraction of the incoming samples can be used for adaptation, leading to lower overall accuracy (Evaluation-TTA, 2023).  We need a TTA algorithm that (1) achieves accuracy close to multi-step approaches such as Tent / EATA / CoTTA, yet (2) adapts in (almost) one forward pass – i.e. converges within a single step and incurs negligible extra wall-clock cost.
idea.methods:
Predictive One-Step Test-Time Adaptation (POSTA)
1. Offline meta-training phase (once, on the source model):
   a. Create a pool of synthetic shifts (ImageNet-C, CIFAR-C, style transfer, RandAugment).
   b. For each mini-batch draw shift x̂.  Run a strong but slow adaptor (e.g. 5-step Tent) on the frozen model’s BN affine parameters (γ,β) and record ∆γ*, ∆β* that give the best post-adaptation accuracy.
   c. Collect the corresponding lightweight "state" s = [µ_batch, σ_batch, entropy(logits)] for each BN layer.
   d. Train a small hyper-network hϕ that maps s → (∆γ*,∆β*).  Loss = L2( hϕ(s) , (∆γ*,∆β*) )  + KL(pred_after_hϕ , pred_after_Tent).
   e. Freeze hϕ.
2. Online test-time phase:
   a. For every incoming batch xt  (size≥16):
      i.   One forward pass through the model in training mode to collect current batch statistics and logits.
      ii.  Feed the stats s into hϕ and instantly obtain ∆γ,∆β – one tensor per BN layer.
      iii. Update BN affine parameters: γ←γ+∆γ , β←β+∆β (no gradient).
      iv.  Re-run the model (or cache activations and only re-apply BN) to obtain final predictions.
   b. Optionally keep EMA of parameters across batches to prevent drift (like PeTTA).

Differences to prior work:  
• Uses a meta-learnt predictor, not gradient descent, eliminating the backward pass.  
• Produces layer-wise closed-form parameter deltas conditioned on current statistics, giving one-step convergence.  
• Can be plugged into any BN-equipped CNN without retraining the backbone.

Implementation: extend the official Tent repo; add HyperBN module that stores hϕ parameters (two-layer MLP per BN) and a controller that performs Steps 2a-2b.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C (severity 5) and ImageNet-R (domain shift without corruptions).  Models: ResNet-26 (CIFAR) and ResNet-50 (ImageNet) pretrained on clean data.
Baselines: 1) Source only, 2) BN (AdaBN), 3) Tent (1-step & 5-step), 4) EATA, 5) CoTTA, 6) PeTTA.  All baselines use their public code & hyper-params.  
Metrics: (i) Accuracy, (ii) Throughput (images/s on single V100), (iii) Realistic stream accuracy (Evaluation-TTA protocol with stream rate r=200 img/s).  
Ablations: remove EMA, vary hyper-network size, compare different training shifts, and test episodic vs continual.
idea.experimental_code:
# simplified implementation skeleton (extends Tent)
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from copy import deepcopy

class HyperBN(nn.Module):
    """Per-layer predictor hϕ_l:  s_l=[mu, sigma, H] → ∆gamma, ∆beta"""
    def __init__(self, bn_layer, hidden=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn = bn_layer
        inp = 3  # mu, sigma, entropy per channel (aggregated as mean)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(inp, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, 2))
    def forward(self, stats):
        # stats: tensor shape [C,3]
        delta = self.mlp(stats.mean(dim=0))
        dg, db = delta[0], delta[1]
        self.bn.weight.data.add_(dg)
        self.bn.bias.data.add_(db)

class POSTA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model, hypernets):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model.train()  # keep BN in training mode
        self.hnets = hypernets      # list of (module_path, HyperBN)
    @torch.no_grad()
    def forward(self, x):
        # first pass – collect stats
        stats = {}
        hooks = []
        for name, hbn in self.hnets:
            layer = dict(self.model.named_modules())[name]
            def save_stats(_, inp, out, key=name):
                mu = out.mean([0,2,3])
                sigma = out.std([0,2,3])
                H = -(out.softmax(1) * out.log_softmax(1)).sum(1).mean(0)
                stats[key] = torch.stack([mu.mean(), sigma.mean(), H])
            hooks.append(layer.register_forward_hook(save_stats))
        _ = self.model(x)
        for hk in hooks: hk.remove()
        # one-shot parameter prediction
        for name,hbn in self.hnets:
            hbn(stats[name].unsqueeze(0))
        # second forward produces adapted predictions
        return self.model(x)

# usage
# 1. load pretrained ResNet-50
# 2. attach HyperBN to every nn.BatchNorm2d layer
model = ...
hnets = []
for name, m in model.named_modules():
    if isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d):
        hnets.append((name, HyperBN(m)))
posta = POSTA(model, hnets)
# inference
for batch in dataloader:
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = posta(batch.cuda())
idea.expected_result:
1. Accuracy: POSTA ≤1% worse than 5-step Tent, higher than 1-step Tent and AdaBN on all datasets.  
2. Throughput: >4× speed-up over Tent/EATA (because no backward pass).  
3. Realistic stream protocol: due to speed, POSTA sees every sample; overall stream accuracy surpasses Tent and matches CoTTA while being faster.  
4. Ablation shows EMA adds ~0.3% accuracy and hyper-network with hidden=16 is sufficient.
idea.expected_conclusion: POSTA demonstrates that meta-predicting BN affine corrections is a viable substitute for iterative gradient-based adaptation, yielding near-state-of-the-art robustness at a fraction of the computational cost.  This bridges the accuracy-speed gap identified by recent TTA evaluations and opens the door to deploying TTA on real-time or resource-constrained systems (mobile robotics, edge devices).  Future work can extend POSTA to non-BN models (e.g., ViT LayerNorm) and regression / detection tasks, or explore joint training of hyper-networks across multiple architectures for universal fast adaptation.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Existing TTA approaches in the related works – Tent, EATA, CoTTA, PeTTA, ITTA, TTAC, etc. – all adapt the deployed model by running on-line gradient descent (one or more backward passes) on an unsupervised loss or by simple running-stat substitution (AdaBN/BN).  None of them meta-learn an explicit predictor that maps current batch statistics to optimal BN affine corrections.  POSTA’s two–stage design (1) pre-computing the optimal multi-step Tent updates for many synthetic shifts and (2) distilling them into a tiny per-layer hyper-network hϕ that produces Δγ,Δβ in a single forward call, eliminates the backward pass altogether.  This differs qualitatively from:  • PeTTA’s divergence-aware regularisation (still SGD).  • CPL’s conjugate loss (still SGD).  • ITTA’s extra adapters updated by gradients at test time.  • Evaluation-TTA paper, which identifies but does not solve the latency problem.  Moreover, no prior work uses BN entropy + (µ,σ) as the state vector for a learned closed-form update.  Hence the method introduces a new paradigm – feed-forward, one-step TTA via meta-learned hyper-BN – that is absent in current literature.
evaluate.significance_reason: Speed is now recognised (Evaluation-TTA, 2023) as the key bottleneck for real-world TTA; slow multi-step methods lose adaptation opportunities on constant-rate streams.  By achieving near Tent/EATA accuracy while being >4× faster and needing only two forward passes, POSTA directly addresses this practical gap, enabling deployment on real-time or resource-constrained platforms (robots, edge cameras, mobile VR).  Academically, it links meta-learning / hyper-networks with test-time adaptation and suggests a principled way to approximate the solution of an optimisation-based adaptor with a learned predictor, opening new research directions (e.g. extending to LayerNorm, vision transformers, detection).  The offline training cost is modest and uses only the source model, keeping the TTA setting intact.  Limitations such as reliance on BN and the need for a corruption pool are present but do not overshadow the potential impact.

idea.open_problems:
1. Existing fast TTA methods are tied to BatchNorm; models with LayerNorm / GroupNorm (ViT, ConvNeXt) or detectors with sync-BN cannot profit.
2. Collecting a large corruption pool for offline meta-training limits deployability and ecological validity.
3. One-shot predictors may drift in long streams because they have no mechanism to gauge their own mistake.
4. Current evaluations ignore energy cost on edge devices, despite speed claims.
idea.methods:
FAST-LANA: Fast Adaptation with Self-Tuned Layer- and Norm-Agnostic Affine modulators.
A. Meta-preparation (once per backbone family)
   1. Replace every normalisation layer (BN, GN, LN) or last conv block with a light Feature Modulator (FM):  y = γ·x+β  where γ,β are produced on-the-fly.
   2. Build a tiny recurrent hyper-network h_φ (GRU-MLP, <20 k parameters).  Its input at time t for each FM is  s_t=[µ_batch,σ_batch, Entropy(logits), ||Δγ_{t-1}||].  Output is Δγ_t,Δβ_t.
   3. Meta-train h_φ by simulating streams with AUTOMATIC shift synthesis: we generate shifts on-the-fly with Fourier based perturbations, style mixing and RandAugment; no curated corruption lists.
   4. Objective: minimise CE on query batch after ONE forward of adapted model + L2 on parameter magnitude + energy proxy E(Δγ,Δβ).
B. Online Phase
   1. For each mini-batch, collect stats, feed to h_φ, update FM weights, predict.
   2. Self-trust gate: if predicted entropy rises or ||Δγ_t||>τ, fall back to EMA of past parameters.
   3. Lightweight rehearsal: keep a 32-sample ring buffer; every 100 batches do one extra forward through h_φ on the buffer to correct drift (still no backward pass).
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets: CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A (natural OOD), and VisDA-C (synthetic→real).  Models: ResNet-50-BN, ConvNeXt-T (GN), ViT-B/16 (LN).  Hardware: Jetson Xavier NX (10 W) and V100.
Baselines: Source, AdaBN, 1-step Tent, 5-step Tent, EATA, CoTTA, PeTTA, POSTA (original idea).
Metrics:
  • Accuracy.
  • Throughput (img/s).
  • Energy per image (J) via NVIDIA-smi power logging.
  • Realistic Stream Accuracy at r∈{50,200} img/s.
  • Drift score (accuracy drop between first and last 10 k samples).
Ablations: (i) remove recurrent connection; (ii) swap entropy with KL to uniform; (iii) ViT without FMs (LN only).
idea.expected_result:
1. Accuracy within 0.5-1 % of 5-step Tent on all shifts; +3-4 % over AdaBN on ViT and ConvNeXt where BN methods fail.
2. 5× speed-up vs Tent, 1.8× vs POSTA (no second forward due to in-place modulation).
3. Energy per image ↓60 % relative to 5-step Tent on Xavier NX.
4. Under Realistic protocol, FAST-LANA sees every sample and achieves highest stream accuracy; drift score <1 % after 100 k images whereas POSTA ≈3 %.
idea.expected_conclusion: A single tiny recurrent hyper-network can deliver zero-back-prop test-time adaptation that is (i) norm-agnostic, (ii) energy-aware, and (iii) robust over long streams.  FAST-LANA removes the BN bottleneck and the need for hand-picked corruption sets, pushing TTA towards practical deployment on real-time, low-power devices and modern architectures such as ViTs and ConvNeXts.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
1. Removes the central BatchNorm assumption that underlies nearly all fast TTA baselines (Tent, EATA, CoTTA, PeTTA, POSTA, etc.) by introducing Feature Modulators that sit on top of BN, LN, and GN alike; none of the cited works adapts LN/GN-based backbones such as ViT or ConvNeXt without back-prop.
2. Generates the modulation parameters with a single tiny recurrent hyper-network that consumes online statistics (µ,σ, prediction entropy, previous ∆) and outputs γ,β updates in one forward pass. Prior one-shot ideas (POSTA) target only BN statistics and do not use a recurrent or norm-agnostic hyper-network.
3. Achieves fully back-prop-free adaptation while still being trainable via meta-learning; existing norm-agnostic attempts (object-detector adaptors, ALEE-style plug-ins) still rely on gradient descent at test time.
4. Integrates an explicit energy proxy into the meta-objective and reports energy/img on edge hardware, whereas the recent ‘Realistic TTA under time constraints’ paper only changes the evaluation protocol and offers no energy-aware learning.
5. Uses automatic, on-the-fly Fourier & style-mix shift synthesis instead of fixed corruption lists (ImageNet-C), removing a common data-engineering bottleneck that none of the listed papers avoids.
6. Adds a self-trust gate plus 32-sample rehearsal buffer to arrest parameter drift without extra backward passes, distinct from PeTTA’s Mahalanobis-based divergence scaling or TTAC’s Gaussian clustering.
Taken together, these elements place FAST-LANA outside the design envelope of the related literature while tackling acknowledged open problems (BN-dependency, speed-vs-energy trade-off, long-stream drift).
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academic: Provides the first evidence that zero-back-prop, hyper-network-driven affine modulation can adapt LayerNorm/GroupNorm models online, extending TTA research to modern vision architectures and giving a new formulation of test-time meta-learning objectives that include energy terms.
Practical: Delivers 5× speed-ups and 60 % energy cut on a 10 W Jetson while matching or exceeding multi-step Tent accuracy; this directly benefits real-time, low-power applications (mobile AR, robotics) where existing BN-based methods are unusable.
Societal: By lowering adaptation energy/latency it supports greener AI deployments and broader accessibility of robust models on commodity edge devices.
Because it simultaneously advances theory (norm-agnostic adaptation mechanism) and practice (deployable on ViT/ConvNeXt with edge-level power budgets), its potential impact is substantial.

idea.open_problems: 1. Fast TTA still depends on norm layers; but modern backbones also contain attention, MLP and convolution blocks whose internal statistics drift. 2. A single hand-crafted state vector (µ,σ, entropy) may not suffice to detect non-covariate shifts such as class prior or semantic drift. 3. Even with FM, per-channel γ,β updates scale linearly with #channels, reducing the speed/energy gain on very wide models (ViT-B/16 has 768-D tokens, Swin-L >1 k). 4. Current energy proxy is heuristic and not tied to hardware-level power counters, giving weak guarantees. 5. No formal guarantee against error amplification; fall-back heuristics may still fail under abrupt or adversarial shifts.
idea.methods:
We propose LANCE (Low-rAnk, Norm- and Component-agnostic Energy-aware adaptation), an extension of FAST-LANA that addresses the above.
A. Universal Adaptive Factors
   • Replace per-channel γ,β with low-rank, token-wise modulators WpWrᵀ (rank r≪C) injected after ANY linear sub-layer (Conv, MatMul, FFN) as y=x+WpWrᵀx.  r=4 keeps <0.5 % extra FLOPs.
   • A single hyper-RNN h_φ outputs ∆Wp,∆Wr given layer summaries.
B. Rich Shift Sensing
   • For every layer we collect a 8-D summary s_t=[µ,σ,Skew,Kurtosis,Entropy,MaxProb,∆losŝ,‖∆θ‖].  ∆losŝ is a one-step look-ahead loss predicted by a tiny zero-cost head trained off-line.
C. Energy-constrained Meta-learning
   • Meta-objective J = CE + λ_E Ê + λ_S ‖∆θ‖² where Ê is estimated Joules via a calibrated regression on NVIDIA power logs; calibration done once per device type (Jetson, RTX).
   • Optimise φ,W* with constrained RL (Lagrangian PPO) to satisfy Ê≤Eₘₐₓ while minimising CE.
D. Drift-safe Controller
   • Maintain an Unscented-Kalman filter on the hidden state of h_φ; if the innovation >δ we revert to last safe parameters and enlarge process noise → faster re-stabilisation.
E. Dataset-free Meta-training
   • Synthetic streams built online using styleGAN-based texture remix + frequency-domain weather engine; no pre-saved corruption lists.
F. Optional Federated Refinement
   • Edge devices periodically send 16-byte sketches (ema of s_t) to update φ without raw data.
All components run in PyTorch and TorchScript for edge deployment.
idea.experimental_setup:
Backbones: ResNet-50-BN, ConvNeXt-T (GN), ViT-B/16 (LN), Swin-T.
Tasks: Image classification on ImageNet-C/R/A, VisDA-C; semantic segmentation on Cityscapes → ACDC-Snow (to test non-covariate, winter shift).
Protocols: Realistic TTA (r∈{50,200} img/s) + new Harsh-Jump (abrupt snow→fog→night every 2 k frames).
Metrics: Top-1, mIoU (seg), Throughput, Energy/img, CO2-eq (via codecarbon), Drift-Δ, Recovery-time after jump.
Devices: Jetson Xavier NX (10 W), RTX-A4000 laptop (mobile).
idea.expected_result:
• ≤0.7 % drop vs 5-step Tent on all shifts; >3 % gain over FAST-LANA on sudden jumps.
• 7× speed-up and 65 % energy saving vs 5-step Tent; 15 % extra saving over FAST-LANA due to low-rank factors.
• First fast TTA to keep ViT-B within 9 W average on Xavier; meets 10 W power envelope.
• After a synthetic snow→night jump, accuracy recovers within 150 images (vs 600 for FAST-LANA, >2000 for Tent).
• Federated refinement improves average OOD accuracy by +0.6 % after 3 edge rounds, with <5 kB uplink.
idea.expected_conclusion: LANCE demonstrates that low-rank, component-agnostic modulators controlled by an energy-aware hyper-RNN enable reliable, green and drift-safe test-time adaptation on modern architectures—even under abrupt non-covariate shocks—without any backward pass. It extends the TTA toolbox beyond norm layers, integrates formal energy constraints, and shows how federated sketches can continually refine adaptation without sharing data, pushing TTA towards scalable, privacy-respectful deployment on heterogeneous edge hardware.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
LANCE tackles the recognised speed bottleneck of Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) with a combination of ideas that do not appear in any of the surveyed works.
1. Parameterisation: Prior fast TTA methods (Tent, EATA, FAST-LANA, PeTTA, RoTTA, etc.) restrict updates to normalisation affine parameters or to small per-block MLP adapters trained with back-prop. LANCE introduces post-layer low-rank modulators y=x+WpWrᵀx that are (i) norm-layer–agnostic, (ii) usable after attention, MLP and convolution, and (iii) driven by a hyper-network so that adaptation is done in a single forward pass—no work in the list leverages low-rank token-wise updates or hyper-RNN-generated deltas.
2. Shift sensing: The 8-dim summary vector augments mean/variance with skew, kurtosis, entropy, predicted loss and parameter drift; existing divergence measures (e.g.
Mahalanobis in PeTTA or entropy in Tent) are lower-dimensional and do not include a learnt loss predictor.
3. Energy-aware objective: LANCE is the first TTA method to include a calibrated hardware-level energy proxy inside a meta-learning loop and to enforce a power budget during adaptation; earlier ‘Realistic TTA’ only measures latency ex-post and does not optimise for it.
4. Formal safety layer: An Unscented-Kalman filter rollback mechanism that gives probabilistic guarantees against error amplification is absent from all compared papers.
5. Dataset-free synthetic meta-training and 16-byte federated sketches address data privacy and storage constraints not considered by prior TTA studies.
Together these elements produce a method that is both conceptually and technically distinct from the state-of-the-art.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, LANCE generalises the scope of fast TTA from BN-centric CNNs to current norm-free or LayerNorm-based architectures (ConvNeXt, ViT, Swin), a gap recently highlighted by the ‘Evaluation of TTA under computational constraints’ paper.  The low-rank formulation keeps FLOPs constant w.r.t. channel width, making the technique scalable to high-dimension token representations – a practical obstacle for transformer models.
The built-in energy constraint and edge-level evaluation align the method with real deployment needs (mobile GPUs ≤10 W), addressing societal pressure for greener AI and widening the range of devices that can benefit from online robustness.  Federated refinement additionally speaks to privacy regulations.
If the reported empirical gains (7× speed, 65 % energy saving, <0.7 % accuracy drop) reproduce, the impact on both research (new adaptation design space, formal resource constraints) and industry (always-on models on low-power hardware) would be substantial.
Limitations – reliance on a hyper-RNN and UKF increases implementation complexity, and formal guarantees are still heuristic – temper the overall significance but do not outweigh the contributions.
